client: I've been feeling overwhelmed lately. It's like there's a weight on my chest that doesn't go away, even when things seem okay on the surface.
therapist: Your experience sounds truly heavy and persistent. When life feels overwhelming, it can be hard to find relief even during calmer times. What do you think might help create some space from this feeling?

client: I appreciate your understanding. Maybe exploring my hobbies or spending time with supportive friends could help ease the pressure.
therapist: Exploring hobbies and spending time with supportive friends are wonderful ways to nurture yourself. How might engaging in these activities shift your story and bring lighter moments into your daily life?

answer_final: I'm sorry to hear that. It's rough to get stressed. Would you like to tell me what's going on?
client: I think immersing myself in my hobbies and reconnecting with friends could provide a much-needed break from the stress. It might help me feel more balanced.
therapist: Immersing yourself in your hobbies and spending time with friends can be a great way to create balance. How do you envision integrating these activities into your routine to enhance your sense of calm and well-being?

user: Sure. I just failed a huge test in my college class, and I'm worried it will fail me the entire class, and then I won't be able to get my associates
answer_final: Oh no! I can totally understand why you're stressing over that! Absolutely valid reason for anxiety.. May I ask how much of the whole grade was the test's percentage?
client: I could definitely spend more time with friends to unwind. But right now, I'm stressed about a recent test I failed in college. It's really worrying me about passing the class and getting my associate's degree.
therapist: You’re feeling the pressure from that test result, which is understandable. Balancing this stress with time for yourself and friends could help. Consider the strengths you've shown in overcoming challenges before—how might they assist you now?

user: Yeah it's really weighing down on me. It's the only thing I can think about. The test was worth 75%
client: It's daunting, especially since the test counted for 75% of my grade. Focusing on past strengths might remind me I can push through and balance this stress.
therapist: Reflecting on your strengths can be a powerful way to regain balance. As you focus on these, how might they offer support in moving through this challenging time and toward your academic goals?

user: I got a 62% on the test.
answer_final: That isn't TECHNICALLY a failed grade by the standards of most professors. Albeit a low grade, it's a D. Anything below 59% would qualify as failed.
client: I scored 62% on the test, and it's stressing me out. Maybe drawing on my persistence and problem-solving skills can help me bounce back from this and refocus.
therapist: Drawing on your persistence and problem-solving skills can be empowering in overcoming this stress. How might applying these strengths help you feel more confident in navigating your path toward the associate's degree?

user: Yeah, but taking into account my scores on homework, I don't think it's enought to pass the class
answer_final: Have you done fairly well in other classes? How have your grades been prior to this test in that class?
client: I've been worried because even with decent homework scores, they won't outweigh the test impact. Maybe using my problem-solving skills to devise a study plan can help turn this around.
therapist: Your willingness to devise a study plan shows your resourcefulness. Trusting in those skills can be grounding. What small, achievable step could you take to feel more assured about your progress and lighten the stress?

user: Honestly it's just kind of all over the place. I am surviving in other classes, but with all this online stuff with the pandemic I barely learn anything. I'm basically faking it til I make it. Which I hate. But I can't learn in these conditions.
answer_final: I hate that you feel that way about yourself, but I can also relate to having a rough time learning via online classes. I'm the same way. However, that does not disable you from being able to learn. It impedes your quality of learning, no doubt. But it isn't something that YOU can help.. By having an attitude of being unable to learn, you automatically lower your expectations for the success you would potentially have otherwise...
client: I think a small step could be setting daily study goals. Honestly, though, everything feels overwhelming right now with this online learning. I'm barely holding it together. The environment isn't helping my focus or motivation.
therapist: Online learning can be demanding, and it seems like the stress is trying to cloud your persistence and focus. By naming these distractions, we can understand their impact on your motivation. Could identifying specific influences allow you to regain control and bolster your study efforts?

user: Yeah that's true, I just think it's not my learning style so it's a lot harder for me. I thought about waiting until things are normal enough to physically be able to go back to class before I try and finish my bachelors, but who knows when that will be
answer_final: OMGoodness no kidding. This whole pandemic has the world in a tizzy!
client: I do struggle more with online learning, as it doesn't suit my style. It's tempting to wait for in-person classes, but delaying might affect my goals.
therapist: Delaying may challenge your goals, yet acknowledging online learning hurdles is vital. Exploring practical adjustments to align with your learning style could gradually enhance focus and motivation. How might small, intentional steps foster the momentum toward achieving your ambitions while maintaining balance?

user: Yeahhh. Honestly just talking to someone and letting it out was kinda nice. made me feel ebtter
answer_final: If I were you I would not wait! It may not be the best option for your learning style, and it will certainly prove a greater challenge. However, taking on that challenge will bring on SWEETER rewards when you succeed! Adopt a "Can-Do" state of mind and grab the bull by the horns!. You're so very welcome!
client: Talking about all of this has been helpful—it’s like a weight lifting, even if just a little. Maybe finding ways to apply that same relief to my study routine could work.
therapist: Finding ways to bring that sense of relief into your study routine sounds promising. What might feel manageable and comforting to incorporate right now, even as you navigate these challenges?

client: Finding a quiet spot at home and breaking study time into short, focused sessions might help. Listening to calming music could ease some stress during breaks.
therapist: Finding a quiet spot and introducing calming elements like music reflects your commitment to creating balance. What value or hope within you might be guiding this effort to ease the stress and stay connected to your goals?

client: I think it's the fear of falling behind. It pushes me, but it’s exhausting too. I just don’t want to regret not giving my best when this is over.
therapist: Fear seems to push you while also draining your energy. Naming it apart from yourself can help lessen its grip. How do your values—like giving your best—offer strength in shaping a way forward amidst this pressure?

client: My values remind me I’m capable, even when fear tries to undermine me. Remembering past successes—like acing a tough project—helps me see I’ve overcome challenges before.
therapist: Your ability to anchor yourself in past triumphs speaks to the strength of your values. How might revisiting these memories more intentionally give you greater leverage against the fear that tries to overshadow your progress?

client: I could start journaling about moments I’ve felt capable, like leading my team at work under pressure. Reliving those might remind me I can handle tough situations again.
therapist: Journaling those moments could help separate fear from your sense of capability. What do those memories tell you about the strengths or values you rely on when pressure arises?

client: Those memories remind me of my adaptability and determination. Like when I revamped a failing project at work by innovating new strategies under tight deadlines. It boosts my confidence.
therapist: Your determination shines through your ability to innovate under pressure. Naming and understanding this can support your efforts in separating fear from self-doubt, focusing instead on those strengths. How does that adaptability resonate with the values guiding you forward?

client: My adaptability feels tied to my value of perseverance. Like during a personal crisis last year, I adjusted priorities and found solutions despite feeling overwhelmed. It reaffirms my strength.
therapist: Your perseverance and adaptability show a commitment to overcoming challenges despite discomfort. If we consider overwhelm as an external force, how might these strengths help you counter its influence while staying connected to the values driving your efforts?

client: I can define current obstacles and treat them as temporary barriers. Recently, organizing weekly meetups despite financial constraints reminded me of the impact of clear priorities on my goals.

client: I think using honesty with my family, especially when discussing disagreements or misunderstandings, can strengthen our bonds. Though scary, expressing my emotions usually leads to productive conversations and better understanding.
